result.summary: Venulus asks Diomedes for help for Turnus, but Diomedes refuses and tells how Venus turned Agmon and his companions into birds after Agmon defied her. Venulus then passes a cave where an Apulian shepherd who mocked the Nymphs was turned into a wild olive tree.

scenes.title: War between Æneas and Turnus
scenes.summary: Caieta is buried, Æneas sails to Latium and is drawn into war with Turnus. Both sides seek allies, and Venulus goes to Diomedes.
scenes.stakes: Æneas and Turnus risk defeat in a doubtful war over Latinus' daughter.

scenes.title: Diomedes tells of Agmon
scenes.summary: Diomedes refuses aid and recounts his sufferings after Troy. When Agmon defies Venus, he and companions become birds.
scenes.stakes: Diomedes' men risk Venus' wrath; Agmon and others lose their human forms.

scenes.title: The shepherd turned olive
scenes.summary: Venulus passes a cave of Pan once held by Nymphs. An Apulian shepherd mocked them and became a wild olive.
scenes.stakes: The shepherd risks punishment for insulting the Nymphs.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Venus, linked with the island Cythera.
Diomedes came from Ætolia and is called its hero.

notable_quotes.reason: Agmon's bitter reasoning that extreme misery frees one from fear.

analysis.text: Defying the gods brings transformation as punishment, and Venus' lasting anger shows divine grudges outlasting the Trojan War.
The shepherd's change into a bitter olive makes his character visible in the tree, a typical Ovidian link between nature and moral fault.

fun_facts.text: Ancient writers linked the birds of Diomedes to seabirds on islands off Apulia, now called the Tremiti or Diomedean Islands.

language_notes.text: Caieta was Æneas's nurse; the promontory and town of Caieta (Gaeta) were said to take their name from her.
'The Goddess of whom so ill a report has been given' is Circe, whose dwelling Æneas passes; her enchantments were told in the preceding fables.
The Narycian hero is Ajax the Less, who raped Cassandra in Minerva's temple; the goddess's anger then wrecked the Greek fleet.
Caphareus is the Euboean cape where much of the Greek fleet was wrecked on its voyage home, by a false beacon.
Venus's 'former wound' refers to Diomedes wounding her in the hand during the Trojan War.
Cytherea is a name for Venus, from the island of Cythera, where she was worshipped.
Diomedes is called grandson of Œneus, king of Calydon; his father Tydeus was Œneus's son.

context_notes.text: Turnus, king of the Rutulians, had been promised Lavinia, daughter of Latinus, before Æneas arrived.
Diomedes, exiled from Argos, married the daughter of Daunus and settled in Apulia in southern Italy.
Pan, the goat-footed god of shepherds and wild places, often occupied caves once sacred to Nymphs.

literary_notes.text: Greek suffering was so great that even Priam, Troy's ruined king and Greece's enemy, would pity it.
Fear is imagined as something that can be trampled underfoot, making Agmon's despair sound like defiance.
The transformation is described limb by limb, a gradual and vivid bodily change typical of Ovid.
The tree's bitter fruit becomes a lasting emblem of the shepherd's own character, so his punishment matches his offence.
